Al-Andalus. The Islamic civilization that dominated the Iberian Peninsula from seven eleven until its final fall in fourteen ninety-two represented over seven centuries of Muslim rule in what is now Spain and Portugal. Established after Arab and Berber forces invaded from North Africa under the Umayyad Caliphate, Al-Andalus became one of medieval Europe's most sophisticated and cosmopolitan societies, renowned for its advances in science, philosophy, mathematics, medicine, and poetry.

Arab and Berber forces led by Tariq ibn Ziyad invaded the Iberian Peninsula in seven eleven, allegedly invited by internal Visigothic factions, and rapidly conquered most of the peninsula within a few decades. Al-Andalus was initially a province of the Umayyad Caliphate centered in Damascus, but when the Umayyads were overthrown by the Abbasids in seven fifty, an Umayyad survivor, Abd al-Rahman the First, established the Emirate of Córdoba lasting from seven fifty-six to nine twenty-nine. By the ninth and tenth centuries, Al-Andalus was more prosperous, populous, and culturally advanced than much of Christian Europe, with major cities like Córdoba, Seville, and Granada rivaling Constantinople and Baghdad.

The Caliphate of Córdoba from nine twenty-nine to ten thirty-one was Al-Andalus's peak. Córdoba was one of the world's largest cities, with a population exceeding four hundred thousand, and a center of learning rivaling Baghdad. Al-Andalus became a center of translation and transmission of classical learning as Greek and Roman texts were translated into Arabic, preserving knowledge that had been lost in medieval Europe, and these works were later retranslated into Latin during the twelfth-century Renaissance. Major intellectual figures included Al-Ghazali, Averroes who was also known as Ibn Rushd as both philosopher and physician, Maimonides the Jewish philosopher, Al-Zahrawi the surgeon and inventor, and numerous poets, mathematicians, and astronomers.

Al-Andalus practiced a system of religious pluralism where Christians, Muslims, and Jews coexisted, paying taxes and maintaining their communities, though Muslims held political power. The Jewish Golden Age flourished in Al-Andalus as Jewish communities produced the greatest medieval Jewish philosophers, poets, and theologians, including Judah ha-Levi, Solomon ibn Gabirol, and Maimonides, synthesizing Islamic and Jewish thought. This multi-religious civilization was fragile, however, as periods of persecution and violence alternated with coexistence, especially during later periods of political instability.

After the Caliphate of Córdoba's collapse in ten thirty-one, Al-Andalus fragmented into numerous petty kingdoms called taifas, weakening Islamic unity and allowing Christian kingdoms of the north including Castile, Aragon, Portugal, and León to gradually reconquer territory. The Reconquista was a centuries-long Christian reconquest, accelerating after the twelfth century as Christian kingdoms defeated Muslims at major battles like Las Navas de Tolosa in twelve twelve, progressively reducing Islamic territory. By the fifteenth century, only the Nasrid Emirate of Granada remained as an Islamic polity in Iberia, a relatively small but wealthy and cultured state.

The Catholic Monarchs Isabella the First of Castile and Ferdinand the Second of Aragon united their kingdoms through marriage and launched the final campaign against Granada from fourteen eighty-two to fourteen ninety-two. Granada fell in January fourteen ninety-two after a long siege, marked by the surrender of the last Muslim king Muhammad the Twelfth, ending Islamic rule in Western Europe and completing the Christian reconquest. The fall of Granada triggered the Spanish Inquisition's persecution and expulsion of Muslims and Jews, with Muslims given the choice to convert, leave, or face execution, while many Jews were expelled to Ottoman territories.
